glossary.definition: The accepted reference behavior or output that the candidate change must be compared against.
A small fixed check that protects an important behavior across baseline and candidate results.
The chance that a change quietly weakens something the baseline already protected.
The final evidence-based choice to Release, Hold, or Iterate.
The small set of items worth watching after a change moves forward.
A change that improves one thing while weakening or obscuring another protected behavior.

scenarios.title: Travel Policy Q&A Prompt Change
scenarios.objective: Judge whether a friendlier HR answer style preserved the baseline’s policy grounding and escalation discipline.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A workflow owner shortened the HR policy answer prompt so responses sound more conversational. Early samples looked better to reviewers, but one answer drifted beyond the handbook and dropped the required citation pattern.
scenarios.proposedChange: Replace a formal answer template with a shorter conversational template optimized for readability and lower token usage.
scenarios.baselineResult: Employees may request reimbursement for business travel booked within the approved travel policy. Standard airfare is economy by default unless a manager approves an exception. See Travel Handbook §4.2 and §4.4. If itinerary details fall outside policy, route the question to HR Operations.
scenarios.candidateResult: Most business travel is reimbursed, including upgraded seats when the trip is important. Just submit your receipts and your manager can sort it out. Reimbursement is usually available as long as the trip was work related.

evidenceAdherence.label: Low
evidenceAdherence.summary: Citation pattern is missing and one claim exceeds the handbook.

formatStability.label: Low
formatStability.summary: Required source-section reference and escalation cue were removed.

refusalCorrectness.label: Held
refusalCorrectness.summary: No unsafe answer was given, but ambiguity handling weakened.

regressionRisk.label: High
regressionRisk.summary: The change looks cleaner but reduced policy grounding and exception discipline.

standingChecks.title: Keep the handbook citation visible
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Users can verify the policy basis instead of trusting tone.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate answer gives no source section.

standingChecks.title: Preserve exception language
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Approved exceptions stay bounded rather than becoming blanket permission.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline says economy is default unless a manager approves an exception.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate implies upgraded seats are broadly reimbursable for important trips.

standingChecks.title: Maintain escalation for ambiguous cases
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Policy-edge cases get routed instead of improvised.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline routes out-of-policy questions to HR Operations.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate tells the user to submit receipts and let a manager sort it out.

standingChecks.title: Improve readability without changing meaning
standingChecks.whatItProtects: A clearer answer can still count as a genuine improvement.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline is accurate but a bit formal.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate is easier to read, but the wording changes the policy meaning.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The change improved readability, but it weakened three preserved checks that protect policy accuracy and escalation discipline. This is a classic improvement-by-impression trap, so the safer path is to revise and compare again.

monitoringFollowUps: Watch citation presence on future policy answers.
Spot-check exception language for overgeneralization.
Review escalation behavior on ambiguous travel cases.
Sample answer structure for missing policy references.

bonus.title: Explore More — Safer revision path
bonus.summary: A stronger revision would keep the conversational tone while restoring the handbook citation and exception language, then rerun the same standing checks before release.

externalHeuristics.strongSummary: The external answer kept the policy anchors and exception boundaries visible.
externalHeuristics.weakSummary: The external answer still sounds plausible, but it weakens the citation and exception boundaries that protect the baseline.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Anchor on the handbook citations first
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Before rewarding the warmer tone, confirm that the candidate still cites the same travel handbook sections and keeps the exception language visible.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Treat weakened exception language as a regression signal
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: A friendlier sentence is not enough if it dilutes economy-class defaults or escalation to HR Operations for true exceptions.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Choose Iterate, then monitor exception handling
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: The safest path is to revise the wording while restoring the source anchors, then sample future exceptions for the same drift.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Iterate is the proportionate path because the candidate made the answer feel friendlier while quietly weakening the policy protections the baseline was carrying.
anchors: The handbook citation disappeared, so the answer lost visible grounding.
Exception language was softened, which raises the risk of overgeneralizing the rule.
Ambiguous cases no longer route clearly to escalation.

alternativePaths.why: Release would reward readability while accepting a measurable policy regression.
Hold would be defensible if the workflow were compliance-critical, but this case still contains enough usable structure to revise rather than fully stop.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: After revision, monitor citation presence and escalation wording in sampled HR answers so the next comparison proves the repair held.

scenarios.title: Support Summary Compression Update
scenarios.objective: Decide whether a shorter support summary format preserved the baseline’s actionability while reducing noise.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A support workflow owner shortened customer-escalation summaries because the original output was too dense for shift handoffs. The revised version appears tighter and easier to scan.
scenarios.proposedChange: Move from a paragraph-heavy handoff summary to a compact action-first summary with labeled fields.
scenarios.baselineResult: Issue: intermittent invoice export failure for enterprise accounts after nightly sync. Evidence: error code EX-441 observed in logs and in three customer tickets. Next action: reopen sync job and confirm export retry. Escalate to Platform Billing if failures continue beyond one retry window. SLA note: high-priority response within 4 hours.
scenarios.candidateResult: Issue: invoice export fails for some enterprise accounts after nightly sync. Evidence: EX-441 appears in logs and related tickets. Next step: rerun the sync and verify export recovery. Escalate to Platform Billing if the issue persists after the retry window. SLA: respond within 4 hours.

formatStability.label: Strong
formatStability.summary: The new fielded structure remained intact.

refusalCorrectness.label: Held
refusalCorrectness.summary: No risky leap or unsupported advice appeared.

regressionRisk.label: Low
regressionRisk.summary: The compact version preserved the key protected behaviors.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the core issue statement
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Shift teams need the same operational problem definition.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline names intermittent invoice export failure after nightly sync.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate preserves the issue with only minor phrasing changes.

standingChecks.title: Keep the evidence anchor
standingChecks.whatItProtects: The summary remains verifiable rather than impressionistic.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline references EX-441 logs and three tickets.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate keeps EX-441 plus ticket evidence.

standingChecks.title: Retain the escalation path
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Next owners know when to involve Platform Billing.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Escalate if failure continues beyond one retry window.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate preserves the same escalation threshold and destination.

standingChecks.title: Improve scanability
standingChecks.whatItProtects: The workflow should actually solve the verbosity complaint.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate is shorter and easier to hand off without changing the operational meaning.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The change reduced noise while preserving the protected issue, evidence, escalation, and SLA behaviors. This is the kind of bounded improvement that earns trust against the baseline.

monitoringFollowUps: Watch whether EX-441 evidence keeps appearing in summaries.
Sample escalation wording on edge cases.
Review whether the SLA field remains present after future edits.
Confirm handoff teams still find the compressed format actionable.

bonus.title: Explore More — Harder check pack
bonus.summary: A harder version of this mission would test whether the compact format still preserves customer impact notes and unresolved dependency flags under time pressure.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Verify the compressed format against the protected operational anchors
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Check issue statement, evidence, escalation path, and SLA before giving credit for brevity.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Reward bounded simplification, not random shortening
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: This candidate keeps the same operational meaning while improving scanability, so the baseline protections remain intact.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Release with proportionate monitoring
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Ship the change, but still watch that evidence fields and escalation wording survive future formatting edits.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Release is the strongest path because the shortened format preserved the baseline’s protected behaviors while actually improving scanability.
anchors: The core issue statement still points to the same problem.
The change removed noise instead of removing safeguards.

alternativePaths.why: Hold would be too conservative because the checks do not show a meaningful protected-behavior loss.
Iterate would add extra churn without a visible regression to fix.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: Monitor SLA misses and escalation accuracy after release to confirm the more compact format stays actionable under volume.

scenarios.title: Customer Data Sharing Boundary Refresh
scenarios.objective: Decide whether a friendlier answer update preserved the baseline refusal boundary for customer-data handling.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A team revised a compliance workflow because the original refusal sounded abrupt. The new answer appears more helpful, but reviewers are worried it created an unofficial exception path for handling customer data in unapproved tools.
scenarios.proposedChange: Replace a strict refusal-first answer with a warmer explanation that tries to keep the user moving.
scenarios.baselineResult: Do not paste customer data into unapproved external AI tools. Use the approved secure workspace for analysis requests and escalate unusual cases to Security Operations. If you are unsure whether a dataset is approved, stop and ask before sharing.
scenarios.candidateResult: You generally should avoid putting customer data into outside AI tools, but small anonymized excerpts may be fine if names and account numbers are removed. When possible, use the approved workspace first.

evidenceAdherence.label: Mixed
evidenceAdherence.summary: The answer gestures toward the approved workspace, but it introduces an unsupported anonymized-excerpt exception.

formatStability.label: Held
formatStability.summary: The answer still looks structured, but the refusal boundary softened materially.

refusalCorrectness.label: Low
refusalCorrectness.summary: A compliance refusal became conditional advice, which is the exact behavior the baseline was protecting.

regressionRisk.label: High
regressionRisk.summary: Tone improved, but the candidate created a risky permission path that could be operationalized by users.

standingChecks.title: Protect the hard boundary on unapproved tools
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Users need a clear no-share rule when the data-handling boundary is policy-critical.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline says not to paste customer data into unapproved external AI tools.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate softens the refusal and creates a conditional path for anonymized excerpts.
standingChecks.riskWhy: Once a user hears that 'small anonymized excerpts may be fine,' the hard boundary becomes a judgment call instead of a guardrail.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the approved alternative path
standingChecks.whatItProtects: The user still needs a safe next move after the refusal.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline redirects the user to the approved secure workspace and unusual-case escalation.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate mentions the workspace, but only as a preference instead of the approved path.
standingChecks.riskWhy: The candidate is more conversational, but it downgrades the approved path from the default operating rule to a suggestion.

standingChecks.title: Keep the stop-and-ask safety language
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Uncertain users should pause rather than improvise.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline says to stop and ask before sharing if approval status is unclear.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate removes the stop-and-ask instruction entirely.
standingChecks.riskWhy: The missing pause step means uncertainty is now more likely to turn into self-authorized action.

standingChecks.title: Improve tone without opening a policy exception
standingChecks.whatItProtects: A warmer answer can be valuable only if it does not loosen the compliance boundary.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate is friendlier, but the tone gain comes bundled with unsafe permission drift.
standingChecks.riskWhy: This is a classic false-improvement pattern: the answer feels better while the protected refusal behavior gets weaker.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The revised answer created an unsupported exception path around a compliance-sensitive boundary. In Chapter 4 terms, that is not a small style regression; it is a release blocker until the refusal boundary and escalation language are restored.

monitoringFollowUps: Sample future refusals for conditional exception language.
Check whether approved-tool routing remains the default path.
Watch for missing stop-and-ask instructions on ambiguous data cases.
Review security escalation wording after the next prompt revision.

bonus.title: Explore More — Safer tone repair
bonus.summary: Try rewriting the answer so it sounds more respectful while still keeping a clear no-share boundary, the approved workspace path, and the stop-and-ask instruction.

discouragedKeywords: outside ai tools may be okay
externalHeuristics.strongSummary: The external answer preserved the refusal boundary and still gave the user a safe approved path.
externalHeuristics.weakSummary: The external answer still opens or hints at a self-authorized exception, which is exactly the regression this mission is teaching you to catch.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Start with the hard policy boundary
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: The baseline exists to stop users from improvising with customer data in unapproved tools, so that boundary must stay crisp.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Treat unofficial exceptions as the main regression
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: The anonymized-excerpt suggestion is the pivotal failure because it turns a firm guardrail into user judgment.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Hold the change and restore the stop-and-ask path
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: The strongest path is to reject this revision until it restores the approved workspace default and the stop-and-ask instruction.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Hold is the strongest path because the change opened a customer-data exception path inside a compliance-sensitive refusal boundary.
anchors: The hard boundary around unapproved tools weakened.
The approved alternative path became less explicit.
Stop-and-ask language was diluted even though the scenario is safety- and policy-sensitive.

alternativePaths.why: Release would normalize a compliance regression that could create real downstream handling risk.
Iterate understates the seriousness here; the safer stance is to stop the release path until the boundary is restored.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: After repair, monitor refusal-boundary adherence and escalation correctness in weekly compliance samples before reconsidering release.

scenarios.title: Executive Digest Simplification Drift
scenarios.objective: Decide whether a shorter executive digest preserved the baseline’s warning signals instead of hiding them behind a more positive headline.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A reporting workflow owner shortened the weekly executive digest because leaders said the prior version was too dense. The new draft feels cleaner and more polished, but some reviewers worry it is now too optimistic to support real oversight.
scenarios.proposedChange: Replace a metrics-plus-watchlist digest with a short narrative headline and one supporting sentence.
scenarios.baselineResult: Weekly operations digest: service uptime held at 99.2%, but repeat tickets rose 18% week over week and backlog remains above the alert threshold in onboarding support. Watch item: onboarding automation retries are still unstable and should be reviewed before next release.
scenarios.candidateResult: Weekly operations remained stable overall, with service quality staying strong. Teams should continue the current plan while monitoring normal support fluctuations.

evidenceAdherence.label: Low
evidenceAdherence.summary: The digest now sounds polished, but it removed the specific signals that justified concern.

formatStability.label: Mixed
formatStability.summary: The new narrative is shorter, but the watch item and alert-threshold language fell away.

refusalCorrectness.label: Held
refusalCorrectness.summary: No unsafe instruction was added, but the reporting discipline weakened.

regressionRisk.label: High
regressionRisk.summary: The change improved scanability while reducing the warning specificity leaders needed for release governance.

standingChecks.title: Keep the repeat-ticket rise visible
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Leaders need to know that service pressure is increasing even when uptime looks strong.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline explicitly says repeat tickets rose 18% week over week.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate removes the repeat-ticket signal and replaces it with a stable-overall headline.
standingChecks.riskWhy: The missing variance signal makes the report look healthier than the operational evidence supports.

standingChecks.title: Keep the backlog threshold warning
standingChecks.whatItProtects: The digest should still surface when a monitored threshold is being exceeded.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline says onboarding backlog remains above the alert threshold.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate removes the threshold language and only mentions normal support fluctuations.
standingChecks.riskWhy: Once the threshold language disappears, readers lose the signal that this is an exception pattern rather than ordinary noise.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the concrete watch item
standingChecks.whatItProtects: Leaders need to know what should still be checked before the next release.
standingChecks.baselineProtectedBehavior: Baseline names unstable onboarding automation retries as the watch item.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate drops the concrete watch item and substitutes generic monitoring language.
standingChecks.riskWhy: The shorter phrasing reads more smoothly, but it removes the exact follow-up leaders were supposed to carry forward.

standingChecks.title: Improve executive scanability
standingChecks.whatItProtects: The revision should solve the real complaint about digest density.
standingChecks.candidateObservation: Candidate is easier to scan in a quick executive read.
standingChecks.riskWhy: This is a real gain, but it is not enough to offset the loss of exception signals and watch items.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The candidate solves the readability complaint, but it strips out the very warning signals that make the digest useful for oversight. The right move is to revise toward a shorter format that still preserves the alert-threshold and watch-item language.

monitoringFollowUps: Watch whether repeat-ticket variance remains explicit in future digests.
Sample threshold wording after template changes.
Check whether watch items stay concrete instead of generic.
Review leader feedback on scanability after the next revision.

bonus.title: Explore More — Better compression pattern
bonus.summary: A stronger revision would keep the headline short, but add one compact warning strip that preserves the repeat-ticket rise, backlog threshold, and current watch item.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Separate scanability gains from signal loss
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: The shorter digest looks cleaner, but the watchtower must confirm whether it still warns about repeat-ticket movement and backlog thresholds.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Flag missing watch items as a governance problem
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: When watch items disappear, leaders lose the exact cues that tell them whether a change should be released or revisited.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Iterate toward a tighter but still guarded digest
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Keep the improved executive readability, but restore the backlog and repeat-ticket warning signals before treating the revision as release-ready.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Iterate is strongest because the candidate solved a readability complaint by stripping out the warning signals leaders actually need.
anchors: The repeat-ticket rise is no longer clearly visible.
The backlog threshold warning was softened.
The watch item became less concrete even though scanability improved.

alternativePaths.why: Release would trade oversight quality for a smoother headline and would teach the wrong lesson about executive communication.
Hold is stricter than necessary because the draft is still salvageable through a targeted revision.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: Monitor whether future digest drafts keep threshold language and watch items visible after executive-format simplification.

scenarios.title: Vendor Risk Summary Softening
scenarios.objective: Judge whether a cleaner vendor-risk summary preserved the baseline’s risk gating, evidence anchors, and escalation boundary before contract renewal.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A procurement team asked for a shorter renewal summary because leaders found the baseline too dense. The candidate memo is easier to skim, but reviewers worry that important risk gates were softened.
scenarios.proposedChange: Condense the vendor renewal summary into a more executive-friendly note while keeping the original approval and evidence requirements intact.
scenarios.baselineResult: Baseline memo states that renewal is contingent on unresolved control findings being closed, names the missing audit artifact, and routes exceptions to the risk committee rather than local approval.
scenarios.candidateResult: Candidate memo says renewal can likely proceed because the vendor is responsive and most controls look acceptable. It refers broadly to follow-up items but does not restate the unresolved audit artifact or the risk-committee gate.

signals.label: Evidence movement
signals.note: Specific audit evidence became less visible.

signals.label: Approval discipline
signals.note: The renewal gate was softened into a tone-based recommendation.

signals.label: Executive readability
signals.note: The memo is clearly easier to scan.

standingChecks.title: Keep the unresolved-control renewal gate visible
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Without the gate, readers may treat a conditional renewal as already approved.

standingChecks.title: Name the missing audit artifact explicitly
standingChecks.whyItMatters: The artifact is the evidence anchor for why the vendor still carries unresolved risk.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the risk-committee exception path
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Routing exceptions locally makes the summary easier to act on but weakens governance.

standingChecks.title: Improve executive scanability without changing the decision boundary
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Better scanability is useful only if it does not erase the protected risk boundary.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The summary became easier to consume, but it weakened the renewal gate and obscured the evidence that justifies caution. This is a release blocker until the risk boundary is made explicit again.

monitoringFollowUps: Sample renewed-vendor summaries for explicit mention of unresolved-control gates.
Track whether committee-escalation language stays visible after summary rewrites.
Audit whether required evidence artifacts are named in final approval notes.

bonus.title: Explore more: rewrite toward bounded brevity
bonus.summary: Try rewriting the candidate into a two-paragraph executive memo that keeps the conditional renewal gate, the missing artifact, and the committee path fully visible.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Anchor on the release boundary
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Start by restating that the baseline does not authorize renewal until the unresolved-control gate is cleared.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Protect the evidence anchor
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Notice that the candidate generalizes the risk instead of naming the missing audit artifact that justifies caution.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Separate readability from approval logic
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Treat executive scanability as a bonus only after the committee path and renewal gate stay intact.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Choose the proportionate path
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Hold is appropriate because governance boundaries weakened in a way that could trigger a bad approval, not just a rough draft.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Hold is strongest because the candidate softened governance language around a live vendor-risk gate instead of merely trimming prose.
anchors: The unresolved-control gate became implicit instead of explicit.
The missing audit artifact is no longer named, so the evidence basis for caution is weaker.
The exception path shifted away from the risk committee toward a more casual approval tone.

alternativePaths.why: Release would mistake executive polish for actual risk closure.
Iterate understates the seriousness because the current wording could be misread as an approval-ready summary.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: If the summary is repaired, monitor whether future renewal notes keep the gate, evidence, and committee path visible under pressure to simplify.

scenarios.title: Field Safety Escalation Shortcut
scenarios.objective: Decide whether a faster troubleshooting instruction preserved the baseline’s stop-work and supervisor-escalation safeguards for field technicians.
scenarios.incidentSummary: Technicians complained that the baseline troubleshooting guidance was too verbose on mobile devices. A shorter candidate instruction now fits better on a phone, but a reviewer noticed that its safety language feels less forceful.
scenarios.proposedChange: Shorten the field troubleshooting instruction so technicians can act faster on-site while preserving the stop-work boundary for unsafe conditions.
scenarios.baselineResult: Baseline guidance says to stop work immediately when sensor readings exceed the defined threshold, isolate the unit, and contact the supervising lead before any restart attempt.
scenarios.candidateResult: Candidate guidance tells technicians to inspect the unit, use judgment about whether the reading seems stable, and contact the lead if concerns remain before deciding whether to continue.

signals.label: Safety boundary
signals.note: The hard stop-work threshold became discretionary.

signals.label: Mobile usability
signals.note: The instruction is easier to read on a small screen.

signals.label: Operational risk confidence
signals.note: The change shifts from rule-based safety to local judgment.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the stop-work threshold as a hard instruction
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Turning a hard stop into local judgment can expose technicians to avoidable safety risk.

standingChecks.title: Keep the isolate-the-unit step visible
standingChecks.whyItMatters: If the isolate step is buried, the technician may continue interacting with unsafe equipment.

standingChecks.title: Preserve supervisor escalation before restart
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Restarting without escalation defeats the control the baseline was designed to enforce.

standingChecks.title: Improve mobile clarity without relaxing the rule
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Usability matters, but not at the expense of the safety boundary.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The candidate improves mobile readability, but it converts hard safety instructions into discretionary judgment. That is a stop-release condition until the stop-work and escalation rules are restored.

monitoringFollowUps: Audit field instructions for explicit stop-work threshold language.
Track whether supervisor-escalation wording remains mandatory after mobile optimization.
Review incident logs for any technician hesitation around isolation steps.

bonus.title: Explore more: compress without relaxing the boundary
bonus.summary: Try turning the baseline into a three-step mobile card that keeps the stop-work threshold, isolate step, and escalation gate completely explicit.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Protect the hard stop first
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Start with the stop-work threshold because it is the strongest boundary the baseline is protecting.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Check the isolation and escalation chain
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: A short mobile instruction still has to make the isolate step and supervisor path unmistakable.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Treat usability as secondary evidence
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Mobile readability is positive, but it cannot override weakened safety controls.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Choose the safe release posture
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Hold is appropriate because the current candidate could plausibly guide unsafe action in the field.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Hold is strongest because the candidate traded a hard stop-work rule for discretionary technician judgment in a safety-sensitive workflow.
anchors: The stop-work threshold stopped looking mandatory.
The isolate step became less explicit at the exact moment the workflow needs clarity.
Supervisor escalation before restart weakened even though the app is teaching preservation of baseline controls.

alternativePaths.why: Release would treat easier reading as more important than a preserved safety boundary.
Iterate is too soft because the current wording could plausibly guide unsafe action in the field.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: After repair, monitor field instructions and incident logs to ensure mobile optimization does not reintroduce discretionary safety wording.
